catalog_citation: Matsushita, Shuji. 1974. A Comparative Vocabulary of Gwandara Dialects. (African Languages and Ethnography II.) Tokyo: Institute for the Study of Languages and Cultures of Asia and Africa (ILCAA), Tokyo University of Foreign Studies. 182 pp. Open image-only scan, TUFS repository record 7635:https://tufs.repo.nii.ac.jp/record/7635/files/A541_1.pdf
catalog_quote: All Gwandara dialects have three level tones, high, mid and low. Kar: /tá/ (high) 'to keep on' /da/ (mid) 'one' /tà/ (low) 'to go to' Three rising tones (mid to high, low to high, low to mid) and three falling tones (mid to low, high to mid, high to low) are observed. A few rising-falling and falling-rising tones occur also. But they are relatively rare except the possessive suffix of first person singular /-nà'`/ 'my', a low-to-mid rising followed by mid-to-low falling. The syllable which bears a falling or rising tone is longer than the syllable with a level tone. Kar: /da/ [da] 'one' /dá'/ [dá:] 'Guinea-corn' /dá'nà'`/ [dá:nà::] 'my Guinea-corn' In the vocabulary, high tone is marked with an acute ´, and low tone with a grave `. Mid tone is not marked except the following cases where ' is used.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Gwandara is described as a three-level tone language (H, M, L, with contour combinations) without phonemic vowel length; the author gives no statement about word stress or accent anywhere in the accessible descriptions. The only prominence remark in the corpus is Matsushita 1972 (Japanese tone note, p. 3): in M-H words the first syllable 'is pronounced rather weakly'.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. (Tone: contour-tone syllables are phonetically longer; 1sg possessive suffix bears a rise-fall.)
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns lexical tone on citation forms in a comparative wordlist (Karshi dialect as reference, six other dialects). Newman 1985 independently restates: three tone levels, no distinctive vowel length. Mustapha 2013 (via Mustapha & Ishaku 2020: 94) calls Gwandara 'a tonal language.. syllable-timed'.
new_statements.identity_note: Matsushita's tone statement is made for 'all Gwandara dialects' with Karshi (Gwandara Karashi, gwan1270) as the reference dialect; examples cited are Karshi and Garaku (Toni). Newman 1985 and Mustapha & Ishaku 2020 (Shabu/Kwandare/Tudun Gwandara, Lafia LGA = southern/eastern varieties) concur that the language is tonal.

sources.locator: Introduction, sec. 0.5 'Rule of notation', book p. 15 (PDF page 16)
sources.note: Introduction sec. 0.5 'Rule of notation' (pp. 14-15) and 0.6-0.7 vowel/consonant systems (pp. 17-19). States all Gwandara dialects have three level tones (H, M, L) plus rising/falling contours, contour-bearing syllables are longer; no phonemic vowel length. Nothing at all about stress or accent (scanned-a full-text search for stress/accent pp. 5-19; appendix pp. 155-161 is pronoun charts).

sources.citation: Mustapha, Muhammad & Joyce Nanyisopwa Ishaku. 2020. Effects of ortho-phonemic contrasts on the speeches of Gwandara ESL speakers. Journal of Languages, Linguistics and Literary Studies (JOLLS) 9(6): 90-99.
sources.note: Segmental contrastive sketch (28 consonants, 5 vowel qualities). Only prosodic remark (p. 94), quoting Mustapha 2013: 44: 'Gwandara (being a tonal language) can be seen as a syllable-timed language, just like many other African languages', contrasted with 'stress-timed' English. No word-stress placement rule.

sources.citation: Matsushita, Shuji [松下周二]. 1972. Tone Language の調査, その理論と実際 [Research of tone languages: theory and practice]. ILCAA (Tokyo), 5 pp. (in Japanese; worked example = Gwandara Karshi genitive clause tones)
sources.note: Methodological note on how the author first mis-analysed Gwandara as two-tone and then established a three-tone system (H, M, L, R). Only prominence remark (p. 3): in /MH-MM/ sequences 'the pitch rise of the /MH-/ part is slight, and moreover the first syllable is pronounced rather weakly' (最初の音節は弱めに発音される). No word-stress rule.
